stem: A push or a pull that can change the state of motion of an object is a __________.
solution: A force is a push or pull that can change an object's state of motion or shape.

stem: The tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or motion is called __________.
solution: Inertia is the resistance of an object to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.

stem: The inertia of an object depends on its __________.
solution: The greater the mass of an object, the greater its inertia.

stem: Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of __________.
solution: Newton's first law is called the law of inertia.

stem: According to Newton's first law, an object continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless __________.
options: acted upon by an unbalanced (net) external force
solution: Newton's first law states an object keeps its state of rest or uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it.

stem: When a moving bus stops suddenly, passengers lurch forward because of their __________.
solution: The passengers' bodies tend to continue moving forward (inertia of motion) when the bus stops suddenly.

stem: When a stationary bus starts moving suddenly, passengers fall backward because of their __________.
solution: The passengers' bodies tend to stay at rest (inertia of rest) when the bus starts, so they fall backward.

stem: The product of the mass and velocity of an object is called its __________.
solution: Momentum = mass × velocity; it is a vector quantity.

stem: The SI unit of momentum is __________.
solution: Momentum (mass × velocity) has the SI unit kg m/s.

stem: Newton's second law states that the rate of change of momentum is directly proportional to the __________.
solution: Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum equals the applied (net) force.

stem: Newton's second law gives the equation __________.
solution: From Newton's second law, force = mass × acceleration (F = ma).

stem: The SI unit of force is the __________.
solution: The SI unit of force is the newton (N); one newton is 1 kg m/s².

stem: A force of 10 N acting on a 2 kg object produces an acceleration of __________.
Newton's third law states that for every action there is an __________.
solution: Newton's third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

stem: The recoil (backward jerk) of a gun when a bullet is fired illustrates __________.
solution: The forward force on the bullet has an equal and opposite reaction pushing the gun backward — Newton's third law.

stem: A rocket moves upward because it pushes gases downward, illustrating __________.
solution: The rocket expels gases downward; the equal and opposite reaction pushes the rocket upward.

stem: When no external force acts, the total momentum of a system is __________.
solution: The law of conservation of momentum: total momentum stays constant when no external force acts.

stem: Two objects colliding conserve total momentum, meaning the total momentum before collision __________ the total momentum after.
solution: By conservation of momentum, the total momentum before and after a collision (in the absence of external forces) is equal.

stem: A heavier object requires __________ force to produce the same acceleration as a lighter object.
solution: Since F = ma, a larger mass needs a larger force to achieve the same acceleration.

stem: When two forces acting on an object are equal and opposite, they are said to be __________.
solution: Equal and opposite forces are balanced; they produce no net force and no change in motion.

stem: An unbalanced force acting on a body causes it to __________.
solution: An unbalanced (net) force changes the velocity of a body, i.e., causes acceleration.

stem: A seat belt in a car protects passengers during a sudden stop by __________.
options: preventing them from moving forward due to inertia
solution: Seat belts hold passengers back, countering the forward inertia during a sudden stop.

stem: A cricketer moves their hands backward while catching a fast ball to __________.
options: increase the time and reduce the force of impact
stop the ball instantly with high force
solution: Moving hands back increases the time of impact, reducing the rate of change of momentum and thus the force on the hands.

stem: The momentum of a 2 kg object moving at 5 m/s is __________.
solution: Momentum = mass × velocity = 2 × 5 = 10 kg m/s.

stem: Which of the following has more inertia?
solution: A loaded truck has the largest mass, so it has the greatest inertia.

stem: The action and reaction forces of Newton's third law act on __________.
solution: Action and reaction forces act on two different bodies, so they do not cancel each other.

stem: Why do action and reaction forces not cancel each other out?
options: They act in the same direction
solution: Though equal and opposite, action and reaction act on different objects, so they do not cancel.

stem: When a book lies on a table, the table pushes up on the book with a force equal to the book's __________.
solution: The table's normal reaction balances the book's weight, keeping it at rest.

stem: A karate expert breaks a slab quickly because a fast blow produces a large __________.
solution: A very quick blow gives a large rate of change of momentum, hence a large force that breaks the slab.

stem: Newton's laws of motion were given by the scientist __________.
solution: The three laws of motion were formulated by Sir Isaac Newton.

stem: Galileo's idea, which led to the concept of inertia, was that a moving object would continue moving forever if there were no __________.
solution: Galileo reasoned that without friction, a moving object would continue moving indefinitely, laying the basis for inertia.

stem: Swimming works on Newton's third law: the swimmer pushes water backward, and the water __________.
solution: By Newton's third law, pushing water backward results in the water pushing the swimmer forward.

stem: A greater force is needed to stop a fast-moving heavy vehicle because it has a large __________.
solution: A heavy, fast vehicle has large momentum, so a greater force is needed to stop it.

stem: If the net external force on an object is zero, the object __________.
options: stays at rest or moves with uniform velocity
solution: With zero net force, an object remains at rest or continues with uniform velocity (Newton's first law).

stem: A person walks forward by pushing the ground backward, and the ground pushes the person forward. This is __________.
solution: Walking is an application of Newton's third law: pushing the ground back, being pushed forward.

stem: The change in momentum of an object depends on the force applied and the __________ for which it acts.
solution: Change in momentum equals force multiplied by the time for which it acts (impulse).

stem: The impulse acting on an object equals the __________.
solution: Impulse (force × time) equals the change in momentum of the object.

stem: A large mass has a large inertia, so it is __________ to change its state of motion.
solution: Greater inertia (large mass) makes it harder to start, stop or change the motion of an object.

stem: A ball on a smooth floor keeps rolling for a long time because there is very little __________.
solution: With little friction to oppose its motion, the ball keeps rolling, consistent with the idea of inertia.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE about mass and inertia?
options: A greater mass means greater inertia
A greater mass means less inertia
solution: Inertia is directly related to mass; a greater mass has greater inertia.

stem: Rockets and jet planes work on the principle of conservation of __________.
solution: Rockets/jets expel gases and gain forward momentum, illustrating conservation of momentum (and Newton's third law).

stem: The unit newton is defined as the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of __________.
solution: One newton is the force that produces an acceleration of 1 m/s² in a mass of 1 kg.

stem: A cushioned or airbag reduces injury in a crash because it __________.
options: increases the time of impact, reducing the force
solution: Airbags/cushions increase the impact time, lowering the rate of change of momentum and thus the force on the body.

stem: Two ice skaters push off each other and move apart; this shows __________.
options: conservation of momentum (equal and opposite momenta)
solution: When skaters push apart with no external force, they gain equal and opposite momenta, conserving total momentum.

stem: An unbalanced force is required to __________.
options: change the speed or direction of a body
keep a body at constant velocity
solution: An unbalanced force is needed to change a body's speed or direction (its velocity).

stem: Dusting a carpet by beating it removes dust because the carpet moves but the dust tends to __________.
options: stay at rest due to inertia and fall off
solution: Beating moves the carpet suddenly while the dust, due to inertia of rest, stays back and falls off.

stem: The product of mass and velocity of a body is its __________.
solution: Momentum = mass × velocity.

stem: A body of larger mass has __________ inertia than a body of smaller mass.
solution: Inertia increases with mass, so a larger mass has greater inertia.

stem: Newton's second law relates force, mass and __________.
solution: Newton's second law gives F = ma, relating force, mass and acceleration.

stem: A rocket works on the principle of conservation of __________.
solution: Rockets gain forward momentum by expelling gases backward, conserving total momentum.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'How Forces Affect Motion' is that:
options: forces change the motion of objects according to Newton's three laws, with inertia, momentum and action-reaction explaining everyday phenomena
forces have no effect on motion
solution: The chapter explains Newton's three laws of motion, inertia, momentum, force (F = ma), and conservation of momentum, applied to everyday situations.
